strengths: The paper targets a relevant limitation of current GCD methods: reliance on global ViT/CLS representations despite fine-grained category discovery often depending on localized cues.

The proposed PartCo framework is simple and broadly applicable: pseudo part labels are constructed from frozen ViT patch features, and the resulting part-level contrastive loss is integrated into several existing GCD methods.

The empirical evaluation is extensive across fine-grained and generic benchmarks, multiple baselines, and DINOv2/DINOv3/CLIP backbones. The gains on SSB fine-grained datasets are substantial, especially for SimGCD, SPTNet, and FlipClass.

The paper includes useful ablations on label order, projection dimension, unsupervised part loss, loss weighting, foreground-only masking, alternative label construction, estimated category count, runtime, and failure cases.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by dataset splits, hyperparameters, compute cost, and label-construction timing, and the limitations section is honest about dependence on patch-token backbones and heuristic PCA labels.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The core method is a heuristic pseudo-labeling pipeline over DINO-style patch features plus a supervised/unsupervised contrastive loss; it is useful, but not a major methodological advance.

The construction of part-level correspondence labels is under-specified in important places: the candidate range for k, handling of empty part groups, normalization details, threshold sensitivity for objectness, and dataset-level choice between first- and second-order labels are not fully operationalized.

The evidence that the discovered clusters correspond to semantically meaningful transferable object parts is mostly qualitative. Quantitative validation against part annotations or correspondence benchmarks would strengthen the central claim.

Some loss notation is ambiguous: projected part features lack explicit image/part indexing, and the denominator in the contrastive losses appears to include only negatives rather than the usual positive-plus-negative normalization, making implementation details unclear.

Main results still assume the number of categories is known, with estimated-K experiments relegated to supplement. Since this assumption is important in GCD, the main claims would be stronger with estimated-K results emphasized more centrally.

The method depends heavily on strong foundation-model patch features and may partly recycle structure already present in DINOv2/DINOv3 rather than learning genuinely new part correspondences. The paper does not fully disentangle this dependency.

No variance over seeds or confidence intervals are reported, despite some generic-dataset gains being small and some old-class accuracies decreasing. This makes it hard to assess robustness of the smaller improvements.
PartCo is not consistently state of the art; for example, it is competitive but slightly below Hyp-SelEx on the SSB DINOv2 average, so claims about setting new benchmarks should be toned down.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant weakness of many GCD methods: reliance on global [CLS] features despite fine-grained category discovery often depending on localized cues. The idea of using patch-level correspondence signals as a training-only prior is plausible and potentially useful.

The empirical section is broad: PartCo is plugged into several baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), tested on fine-grained and generic benchmarks, and evaluated with DINOv2, DINOv3, and CLIP image features. The gains are especially large on fine-grained datasets for weaker baselines, e.g. PartCo-SimGCD improves average SSB All accuracy from 69.0 to 78.8 with DINOv2.

The supplement includes several helpful analyses: projection dimension, label order, unsupervised part loss, foreground-only masking, CLIP backbone, estimated-K settings, runtime overhead, and success/failure cases. The limitations section honestly notes dependence on ViT patch tokens and the limited spatial resolution of the patch grid.
The method has a practical appeal because it adds no inference-time cost and can be attached to existing GCD objectives.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. The core recipe is DINO-style patch features plus PCA/k-means pseudo part labels plus a supervised/unsupervised contrastive loss. Much of the benefit appears to come from distilling strong foundation-model local structure into existing GCD models rather than from a conceptually new category-discovery mechanism.

Key parts of the method are under-specified. The paper says k* is chosen by minimum center distance and cluster-size balance, but does not give a precise objective, search range, thresholds, or deterministic selection rule. The PCA/objectness thresholding also uses a fixed tau=0.6 without explaining normalization of PCA scores or robustness. These omissions make reproduction and fair comparison difficult.

The central claim that PartCo provides semantic part correspondences is not fully established. The constructed labels are unsupervised clusters of patch descriptors, not true parts, and the CUB comparison reports Hungarian-matched alignment only for one dataset before downsampling. There is little evidence that these clusters remain semantically consistent across generic datasets or across backbones.

The evaluation is extensive but not statistically convincing. Results appear to be single runs with no variance, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to random seeds, despite the method depending on sampling labeled images, k-means, pseudo-labels, and clustering accuracy. Some reported gains on strong baselines/generic datasets are small or mixed, e.g. PartCo-SimGCD on generic DINOv2 improves All only 92.4 to 92.7 while New drops 91.3 to 90.4.

The paper overstates significance. It claims to set new benchmarks, but PartCo-SelEx is not clearly state-of-the-art against several recent methods in the main tables: Hyp-SelEx is slightly better on average SSB All with DINOv2, and generic benchmark results are competitive but not consistently dominant.

There are fairness/comparison concerns. PartCo uses an additional offline label construction stage from strong pretrained patch features, while some baselines are reported from prior work and others are reimplemented. The paper does not clearly separate gains from stronger backbones, transductive preprocessing over the unlabeled set, and the proposed loss itself.

The presentation is verbose and sometimes imprecise. Several claims are repeated in broad language, equations use notation that is hard to verify, and the description of first- versus second-order labels relies on informal dataset-type heuristics rather than a principled selection procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are not enough to reconstruct the label-generation pipeline exactly, there is no code release statement in the manuscript, and important hyperparameters for k-means/PCA/label downsampling and pseudo-label construction are missing. Ethics discussion is essentially absent, though risks are modest for this benchmark-oriented vision paper.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and practically useful plug-in framework for GCD: construct part-level correspondence labels from frozen ViT patch features and use them to supervise patch-token part representations via a contrastive loss. The method is easy to integrate with existing GCD objectives and adds no inference-time cost.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. PartCo improves several representative baselines, including SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, and SelEx, across fine-grained and generic datasets, and the gains are especially strong on fine-grained benchmarks such as CUB, Stanford-Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft.

The ablations are unusually thorough for this type of contribution: the paper studies first- vs second-order part labels, projection dimension, supervised vs unsupervised part correspondence losses, balancing weight, computational overhead, CLIP backbones, unknown-K estimation, foreground-only masking, and alternative SD-DINOv2 label construction.

The work gives good evidence that the benefit is not merely background removal: the foreground-only ablation gives much smaller gains than explicit part correspondence learning. The comparison against CUB annotated parts also supports the claim that the constructed labels capture meaningful part structure.

The presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures, quantitative tables, qualitative attention maps, and a concrete limitations section. The computational overhead and label-construction times are reported, which improves practical reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical idea is incremental relative to the growing line of part-aware and patch-token-based GCD methods, including SPTNet, PartGCD, APL, and related part-learning work. The contribution is valuable, but it is more of an effective framework/regularizer than a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

The method depends on high-quality pretrained ViT patch features, and much of the part-label construction is inherited from properties of DINOv2/DINOv3/CLIP. The paper shows robustness across these backbones, but it does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes from PartCo versus the already strong spatial structure of the foundation model.

The choice between first-order and second-order labels is dataset-type dependent, and the paper frames this as straightforward, but in practice this is an additional design decision that may require validation or prior knowledge about whether a dataset is fine-grained or generic. More guidance for automatic selection would strengthen reproducibility and deployment.

Most main experiments appear to report single-run accuracies without confidence intervals or standard deviations. Given that GCD evaluation can be sensitive to clustering, pseudo-labeling, and initialization, the lack of variance estimates weakens the evidential strength of some reported gains, especially the smaller generic-dataset improvements.

The construction pipeline has some ambiguities that could affect reproducibility, such as the exact candidate set for k, thresholding details, whether and how all unlabeled data participate in clustering, and implementation details for cases with missing part categories in a batch. These are likely resolvable but should be specified more explicitly.

The impact statement is generic and does not seriously discuss possible risks of category discovery systems, such as biased discovery from foundation-model representations or downstream surveillance/taxonomy-building applications. There are no obvious severe ethical issues, but the ethics treatment is minimal.
